# Rovaq AI

> Rovaq AI connects conversations, orders and refunds to show where revenue is at risk. Every figure comes with its source and its cut-off date. Always gross revenue, never margin. Exposure is an inferred figure, not a loss.

Content updated: 2026-11-03.

---

## Know how much money slips away, and why.

Post-purchase revenue intelligence for businesses that sell on marketplaces

Rovaq AI measures observed refunds and the revenue exposed to each problem, with the evidence in plain view and every figure labeled Observed, Estimated or Inferred.

Always gross revenue, never margin. Exposure is an inferred figure, not a loss.

### Every problem, with its exposed revenue and its evidence.

A repeated theme is not the same as a theme that costs. Rovaq puts beside each problem its exposed revenue, where it comes from, the date it reaches and what is still unknown.

- Gross revenue, never margin.
- What is unknown says No data, never zero.
- Currencies kept apart, never converted.
- A person decides every action.

### The information that explains your revenue leaks is scattered.

And nobody connects it.

- Three places, no single view. Conversations sit in a support tool, orders and refunds in each marketplace, and reports in spreadsheets.
- A silent leak. Refunds that could be claimed and are not make a silent leak. Without seeing them by channel and by product, there is nowhere to act.
- A deadline that passes. Missed response times show up after the customer has already complained. Knowing when threads arrive makes it possible to staff in time.
- Figures that read as facts. Spreadsheet reports often mix currencies, treat missing data as zero and present estimates as facts.

### Every figure says where it comes from.

### Four classes of figure and a single rule.

- Observed. Recorded at the source, such as orders and settled refunds.
- Estimated. Calculated with a model or with assumptions you define. It is not a recorded fact.
- Inferred. Linked by evidence, such as the revenue of orders tied to a problem. It is not a loss and is not added across problems.
- No data. There are no eligible records. It is never shown as zero.

The rule. Under every important figure goes its seal: class, source, cut-off date and age. If the cut-off date is unknown, the seal says so.

### Four modules, and a person who decides.

Each module does one part of the work with your data. They are not autonomous agents: they propose and prepare, and a person approves every action.

- Import with provenance. Bring in HubSpot conversations and orders or refunds from Excel and CSV. Every record keeps its source and cut-off date. Marketplaces come in by export, with help from our team.
- Group into problems. Each problem shows its volume and evidence when links are confirmed. Emails and phone numbers are masked. See what repeats. Grouping with AI models is enabled per organization.
- Quantify in gross revenue. Each problem shows exposed gross revenue, labeled Inferred and never as a loss. Every figure carries class, source and cut-off. Exposure is calculated only with the problem-to-order links that an owner confirmed.
- Decide and measure. Each recommendation brings its evidence. A person decides: Proceed, Adjust or Dismiss. Nothing is sent automatically; the outcome is recorded. Proceed creates the intervention and drafts that a person reviews and sends.

### Six screens, each built to answer one question.

Walk through the product with example data. No data is from a customer.

- [Today](https://rovaq.ai/en/product/today). What needs attention today. Four key figures based on the sources you have loaded: gross revenue, refunds, stuck money and replies over 24 hours, each with period, formula and coverage.
- Refund leakage. Where returned money concentrates. See where returned money concentrates by channel and product, and download an evidence package. You review it and you file it.
- Problems with evidence. Which problem to prioritize and with which cases. Each problem is presented with its volume and its evidence when links are confirmed. Economic exposure is an Inferred figure: revenue from orders linked to the problem, not a loss.
- [Ask your data](https://rovaq.ai/en/product/ask-your-data). How this figure was reached. Type a question and get figures, tables and charts. It runs on rules, without a language model, shows how it calculated and says when it does not have the data.
- [To decide](https://rovaq.ai/en/product/to-decide). What is proposed and who decides. Every proposal arrives with its evidence and its reason. A person decides: Proceed, Adjust or Dismiss, and the outcome is recorded.
- [Data trust](https://rovaq.ai/en/product/data-trust). How much to trust a figure. A traffic light per source, the freshness of each figure, its coverage and a list of what is still unknown. It is trust in the data, not a certification.

### Each role sees what belongs to it.

- Owner. Configures, decides and approves. Manages team, notices and retention. All screens, the team, notices and retention.
- Analyst. Investigates, prepares and proposes. Sees money and imports files. Money, problems, pain points and imports. Proposes and does not approve.
- Operator. Carries out the actions assigned to them. Sees problems and actions, without money figures. Problems, assigned actions and evidence. No money figures.
- Viewer. Reads with read-only access, with no risk of changing anything. The screens that apply to them, unable to modify data, connections or decisions.

Finance and customer experience read the same problem: the money that is returned and the reason it is returned.

Authorization is decided on the server. Hiding a menu item does not protect a screen.

### Security described by what exists today and what does not yet.

What exists.

- Each organization is kept apart from the others by rules in the database, not only by the application.
- Four roles with least-privilege permissions. The platform administration permission is separate and does not grant read access to the business data of other organizations.
- Sign-in is by a link sent to your email, with email confirmation, and sessions use protected cookies.
- Connections to your sources request read permissions.
- Pain-point and claim exports are generated without personal data.
- Administration operations, team changes and retention deletions are recorded.
- When AI is involved, it classifies and drafts. It does not produce amounts, and a person decides.

What does not exist yet.

- We do not hold SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certification, and we do not claim GDPR compliance.
- No external penetration test has been performed.
- Two-step verification for owners is on our roadmap. It is not required today.
- We do not offer single sign-on or a customer-facing audit view.
- There are daily provider backups, without point-in-time recovery, and we make no availability commitments.

### What Rovaq does not do.

The limits are part of the product too.

- It does not calculate margin or profit. Everything is gross revenue.
- It does not convert currencies or add them. USD, CAD and MXN are kept apart.
- It does not present exposure as a loss. It is an inferred figure and is not added across problems.
- It is not an autonomous agent. It prepares the package and the draft; a person files the claim and decides every action.
- It does not promise recovery, savings or return. What is recoverable is an estimate based on assumptions you enter.
- It does not work in real time. Sync is scheduled and every screen shows its cut-off date.
- It does not connect directly with Amazon, Walmart or Shopify. Today their exports are loaded.
- It does not use a language model to answer in Ask your data and it does not search the internet.
- It holds no SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certification, does not claim GDPR compliance, and two-step verification for owners is on the roadmap.
- It does not replace your support tool. It reads HubSpot conversations in read-only mode and does not write to your CRM.

If anything on this list changes, it will be stated here.

### What connects today and what comes next.

HubSpot, read-only, and Excel and CSV files. Marketplaces come in today through their exports.

Available today.

- HubSpot. Reading of conversations, read-only, with a scheduled sync every 5 minutes. It is not real time and coverage is limited to what the HubSpot API exposes: every screen shows its cut-off date. The connection is set up with our team.
- Excel and CSV. File upload with preview and validation before ingesting. Marketplace exports are loaded with help from our team.

On the roadmap.

- Direct connectors for Amazon, Walmart and Shopify. Today their exports are loaded.
- A full problem map by shipping address, which requires those connectors.
- Two-step verification for owners.

Rovaq does not replace your support tool. It reads HubSpot conversations in read-only mode and connects them with the orders and refunds you load.

### Frequently asked questions

#### What is Rovaq AI?

It is revenue intelligence for businesses that sell on marketplaces and support customers across channels. It connects conversations, orders and refunds, and shows every figure with its class, source and cut-off date.

#### Which sources does it work with today?

With HubSpot, read-only, and with Excel and CSV files. Amazon, Walmart and Shopify are on the roadmap: today their exports are loaded with help from our team.

#### Is the data updated in real time?

No. HubSpot syncs on a schedule every 5 minutes and file uploads are manual. Every figure shows the date its data reaches and how long ago it was updated.

#### Does Rovaq calculate my margin or how much money I lose?

It does not calculate margin: everything is gross revenue. Refunds are observed figures. Exposure per problem is an inferred figure: the revenue of orders linked to that problem, which is not the same as a loss.

#### Does Rovaq use AI and where?

Ask your data answers with rules and read-only tools, without a language model, and shows its steps. Grouping and classifying conversations can use AI models when the organization enables it. AI does not create amounts and a person decides every action.

#### Does Rovaq claim refunds for me?

No. It assembles a package of aggregated evidence and a draft message. You review them and file the claim. Nothing is sent on its own and no recovered amount is promised.

#### How secure is it and what certifications do you hold?

There is isolation per organization in the database, four roles, read connections and a record of administration operations. We hold no SOC 2 or ISO 27001, we have not run an external penetration test and two-step verification for owners is on the roadmap. The detail is on the Security page.

#### Does Rovaq replace my support tool?

No. It reads HubSpot conversations in read-only mode and connects them with the orders and refunds you load. It does not write to your CRM or reply to your customers.

#### How do I request access and what does it cost?

Request access at https://rovaq.ai/en/request-access with your role and the tools you use. We review your case and tell you what can be loaded or connected today. Pricing is not published yet.

### Request access and review your figures with their evidence.

Write to us by email. We tell you plainly what can be loaded today and what is still on the roadmap.

Pricing is not published yet.

## Today: four figures with period, formula and coverage

What needs attention today, with every figure labeled by its class and its source.

### What the screen shows

- Four key figures: gross revenue, refunds, stuck money and replies over 24 hours, each with its period.
- A Needs your attention block with alerts, such as a leak on one product, overdue requests or threads without a reply.
- The Suggested next action and a button to export the report.

### How to read a partial figure

Stuck money comes from an Excel Tracker that is loaded by hand and carries no cut-off date. Replies over 24 hours come from HubSpot. Every figure states its coverage and what is still unknown.

### What it does not calculate

- It does not calculate margin or profit: revenue is gross.
- It does not add or convert different currencies, because there is no approved exchange rate.
- An empty state says there is no data yet and never shows it as zero.

### Who sees it

All four roles, with different views. Owner and analyst see the four figures. Operator and viewer see a view of their own, without money figures.

_Example data. Not from a customer._

## Pain points: which reason repeats and what it carries

Tell what repeats from what costs.

### Bubble map

- Each bubble is a pain point. Its size is returned money in gross dollars or volume, your choice.
- The eight largest appear in the chart and in an accessible table, with a topic filter.
- Each row opens its evidence down to the source row.

### Export without personal data

Export the evidence as CSV per pain point, without personal data. What is not known says No data and never zero.

### What it does not do

- A repeated theme is not a theme that costs: the screen puts the money it carries beside it, when it exists.
- If a source did not respond, those points show as Not available now and not as zero.

## Ask your data: calculated figures, visible steps

How this figure was reached, in plain view.

### How an answer is calculated

You type a question and get figures, tables and charts, each with its class and coverage. Figures come from read-only tools and are calculated with rules, without a language model.

### Steps in view

- Each answer can be opened in How I got here, with the steps, the parameters, the method and the source.
- The steps were recorded by the system; they are not the internal reasoning of a model.
- You can copy, download as CSV, rate the answer and attach a file of up to 1 MB that is analyzed only in your browser.

### What it does not do

- This describes the general agent of this screen. The Finance mode has its own engine and we do not claim it is rules only.
- It does not use a language model to answer and does not search the internet.
- When it does not have the data, it says so and does not invent it. If the question does not match an available query, it asks you to clarify.
- The monthly budget limits queries; when it runs out, direct queries remain.

### Who sees it

All four roles. The operator receives totals and not specific customers.

_Example data. Not from a customer._

## To decide: proposal, a person decides, outcome recorded

What is proposed and who decides.

### The life of a proposal

Each recommendation brings its evidence, why it is suggested and what is expected. A person decides, and the outcome is recorded with its before and after measurement, using observed data only.

### Proceed, Adjust or Dismiss

- Proceed creates the intervention and the drafts that a person reviews and sends. Nothing is sent automatically.
- Adjust and Dismiss ask for a reason, which is recorded. Reopening a dismissed proposal creates a new event and deletes nothing.
- Propose: owner, analyst and operator. Approve: owner only. Carry out: owner and operator.

### Outcome record

In progress shows the owner, the commitment, the stages and the drafts. Outcomes measures before and after and never presents an assumed saving.

_Example data. Not from a customer._

## Data trust: freshness, coverage and what is unknown

How much to trust a figure.

### Freshness and coverage

- A traffic light per source: Up to date, Manual load, Delayed, Alert, Paused or No data.
- The freshness of each figure: when it was recalculated and the date its data reaches.
- Coverage, with windows per channel.
- A How it was calculated panel on each figure, with its origin, period and formula.

### What is still unknown

What we do not know is a task list: the affected figure, what closes it and its basis. A source that never ran appears as No data and not as Up to date. Manual loads do not raise an alert.

### Data trust is not certification

This screen is about the quality of the figures. It is not a security or compliance certification.

_Example data. Not from a customer._

## Finance: a report by currency, bases never mixed

What the report says by currency.

### Gross revenue by currency

- Revenue, orders, refunds and refund rate by currency, with a 12-month series and the mix by channel.
- The monthly comparison only between complete months; incomplete months are dotted.
- A three-month projection with a range, labeled Estimated, which is not shown with fewer than four complete months.

### Cutoffs and reconciliation

Every figure states its currency, basis and period. What is missing appears as a task list and not as a zero. A figure with incomplete reconciliation is flagged as partial. The report is exported as CSV and PDF with the same figures as the screen.

### What it does not calculate

- It does not calculate margin or profit: everything is gross revenue.
- It does not add or convert USD, CAD and MXN, and does not subtract refunds from revenue because they are different bases.
- Exposure per problem shows as Not available until each problem is linked to its orders.

### Who sees it

Owner and analyst. Operator and viewer get a notice that their role has no access to this panel.

_Example data. Not from a customer._

## Owner: configure, decide and approve

Manages team, notices and retention, and approves actions. Approving belongs to this role alone.

### What they configure

- Invites the team by email with a role; invitations expire and give no access until accepted.
- Connects sources with help from our team and authorizes imports.
- Sets the organization notice delivery and the retention and deletion policy, which first shows the exact scope and deletes nothing until confirmed.

### What they decide

- Approves, adjusts or dismisses the proposals in To decide.
- Confirms the problem-to-order links that exposure depends on.
- Publishes the organization order and refund cutoffs.

### What is recorded

Administration operations, team changes and retention deletions are recorded. The platform administration permission is separate and does not grant read access to the business data of other organizations.

Moves the intervention stages, reviews and sends the drafts, and records the outcome. Proposing is also within the role; approving is not.

## Refunds are not a fixed cost: they are a leak you can locate

A single total does not say what to tackle first. By channel, by product and by month, returned money starts to take shape.

Many e-commerce teams treat refunds as a cost of doing business: a percentage that is accepted, budgeted and reviewed once a month. The total goes up or down, someone asks why, and the conversation ends with a general explanation about the season, returns or demanding customers.

That reading has a problem. A single number mixes things that are not alike, and what is not separated cannot be handled. A different stance helps: treat returned money as a leak, something that has a place, a shape and, with some work, an owner.

### Why a single total fails

Imagine the refund total for one month equals the previous month. The comfortable reading is that nothing happened. But that same total can hide that one channel improved while another got worse, or that a single product accounts for almost all the movement while the rest stays steady. Two months with the same total can tell opposite stories.

A total answers how much, but it does not answer where or when, and those are the questions that get someone to act. If the number does not tell you what to open first, all it does is worry you.

> A total says how much. To act, you need to know where, when and with what evidence.

It does not help to compare any month against any month either. A half month against a full one makes everything look like an improvement, or a disaster, depending on the order you put them in. An honest comparison sets complete, comparable months side by side. And when there are not yet two of them, the most useful thing a tool can do is say so instead of drawing a trend that does not exist.

### How to read a refund Pareto

A Pareto is a simple chart: it sorts categories from largest to smallest and shows how much of the total each one adds up to. For refunds, the idea is to pick the axis you want to investigate and see whether a few bars explain a good part of the returned money. No magic ratio has to hold. What matters is that the distribution is almost never even, and the shape of the chart tells you where to begin.

It helps to read it in three cuts, one at a time:

- **By channel.** It shows whether the problem lives in one particular place of sale or is widespread. If one channel concentrates the movement, the conversation is with that channel and its rules, not with the whole business.
- **By product.** It points to which items add up to the most returned money. A product at the top may be a matter of description, packaging or supplier; the cut does not say which, but it tells you whom to ask.
- **By month.** It shows whether the movement is steady, has a spike or is growing. An isolated spike and a sustained climb call for different answers.

Then cross the cuts with each other. A product that dominates in one channel tells a different story from one that dominates in all of them. And look at repeated contact too: customers who write more than once about the same matter often point to something the first message did not resolve.

#### What a Pareto does not tell you

It orders the money, but it does not explain the cause. With an export of orders and refunds you usually cannot calculate the refund rate per product, margin or net loss, because the columns needed to do it rigorously are missing. A Pareto tells you where to look. The reason is yours to supply, through conversations, inspection and judgment.

### What an evidence package contains

Locating the leak is half the work. The other half is being able to back what you found in front of whoever has to decide: a supplier, a carrier, an internal team. A claim without support gets argued; one with support gets reviewed.

No matter which tool you build it with, a useful evidence package answers, in order, what the other party is going to ask:

- Which product and which period it covers, so nobody argues about the scope.
- How many refunds there were and for how much money, with the source and cut-off date of each figure.
- The detail order by order, so each line can be checked one by one.
- The recorded reasons and, when they exist, the related conversations.
- The assumptions used to size the claim, written down by whoever chose them.

In Rovaq AI, the refund leakage screen generates an evidence package per product, as HTML and CSV, and a list of products for the supplier. Everything is built in your browser and the screen confirms that nothing was sent: you review the package and you file the claim.

### How to start with what you already have

You do not need a big project. Take an export of orders and refunds from the last complete months and put three questions to it, in order. Which channel concentrates the most returned money? Which products lead that channel? Is that new, or was it already there the month before? With those three answers you have a place to look, which is more than a total gives you.

Then decide who owns each finding. A leak without an owner turns back into a fixed cost, and the cycle starts over. And before moving money or writing to a supplier, check where each figure comes from and what date it reaches: [data trust](https://rovaq.ai/en/product/data-trust) is checked before deciding, not after.

### What we do not claim

- We do not claim that every refund is a leak. Many are legitimate returns and should stay that way.
- We do not promise any amount. Any estimate of how large a claim could be depends on the assumptions you write.
- We do not calculate the refund rate per product, margin, net loss or root cause from an export, because the data needed to do it is missing.
- Nothing is sent on its own: a person files the claim.

Fuente: https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/where-every-number-comes-from

## Where every number comes from: provenance as a requirement, not decoration

A figure without an origin can only be accepted or rejected. With its source, its cut-off date and its gaps in plain view, it can be debated.

Almost every team has lived the same scene. Someone opens a dashboard, sees a figure they did not expect and asks where it comes from. Nobody knows for sure. The formulas get checked, the author of the report is tracked down, the number is compared against a spreadsheet and, in the end, the meeting is spent finding out whether the figure is true instead of deciding what to do about it.

The idea fits in one sentence: provenance is not a decoration added at the end to make a good impression, but a requirement met before a figure is shown. A number that cannot explain its origin is not data, it is an opinion with formatting.

### A dashboard that demands belief

A traditional dashboard presents clean results: a large figure, a chart, a change against the previous period. That cleanliness is useful for a quick look, but it hides everything needed to doubt with judgment. It does not say whether the number comes from a record, an estimate or a calculation made with assumptions. It does not say which day the data reaches. It does not say which part of the business was left out.

When those answers are missing, the reader has two options, and both are bad. They can accept the figure out of courtesy toward whoever presents it, or reject it out of general distrust. In neither case are they evaluating the number: they are evaluating the person or the tool that shows it.

> A figure that does not explain its origin demands belief. A figure with provenance can be debated.

### Cut-off date, source and gaps

For a figure to be debatable, four things need to travel with it. In Rovaq AI we call them the figure seal, and it accompanies the important figures on the screens that show it.

- **The class.** A figure can be observed, meaning a recorded fact; estimated, calculated with a model or with assumptions you define; inferred, derived from other relationships; or it can be No data. Mixing those classes in one column is the most common way to fool yourself without meaning to.
- **The source.** Which file, which system or which load the record comes from, so that anyone in doubt can go and look.
- **The cut-off date.** Which day the data reaches. A figure correct up to the fifteenth and one correct up to the thirtieth are not the same figure, even if they share a name.
- **The age.** How much time has passed since the last update, so nobody mistakes an old snapshot for today.

The rule that holds everything else up is this: if the cut-off date is not known, the seal says so. The same goes for any missing data. What is unknown is shown as No data, never as zero. A zero asserts that something was measured and nothing was found; a missing value admits that it is not known. The difference seems small until someone makes a decision believing a category has no activity when, in fact, nobody loaded its records.

#### The ledger that keeps corrections

Provenance also depends on how the data is stored. In Rovaq AI each organization has an insert-only ledger: when something is corrected, a revision is added and the earlier version is not erased. That way, a correction leaves a trail instead of quietly rewriting history, and whoever reviews can see that a change happened and when it was made. The exception is retention: the policy each organization defines can delete data, and that deletion is recorded.

### Data trust versus outside endorsement

Two things that are often confused are worth separating. Data trust answers a practical question: how much can I rely on this figure today. A certification answers another: whether an organization meets a certain standard, verified by a third party. They are different matters and neither replaces the other.

The [data trust](https://rovaq.ai/en/product/data-trust) screen exists for the first. It shows a traffic light per source, the freshness of each figure, its coverage and a list of what is still unknown. It is a tool for everyday work: before moving money or writing to a supplier, whoever decides can see which sources are up to date, which fell behind and which gaps remain open.

The second, certification, is a different conversation, and we have it plainly: Rovaq AI does not hold security or compliance certifications today. A trust screen does not try to take that place. What it does is leave the real state of each source in plain view, which is what a team needs to work with figures without going blind.

### A simple test for your own dashboard

You do not need to adopt any tool to start demanding provenance. Take the three figures that weigh most in your decisions and put these questions to them, out loud and in front of whoever prepares them:

1. Which file or system it comes from, and who can open it to check.
2. Which day the data reaches and when it was last updated.
3. Whether it is a recorded fact, an estimate or an inference, and who wrote the assumptions when there are any.
4. Which part of the business was left out and how that absence is being shown.

If the answers arrive quickly and agree with one another, the dashboard earns its place. If they take effort, you already have a list of what is worth fixing before the next meeting. In either case the conversation improves: it stops being about whether the number is true and starts being about what to do with it. A good example is refunds, which we covered in [this article on leaks in returned money](https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/refund-leak-you-can-locate), where every total is worth only as much as its origin.

### What we do not claim

- We do not claim that a figure with provenance is correct. Provenance makes it possible to review it; it does not make it true by itself.
- We do not claim that the data trust screen is a certification or that it replaces an audit.
- We hold no security or compliance certifications, and we do not suggest otherwise.
- We do not treat unknown data as zero: if it is missing, the seal says No data.
- We do not promise that data is current at every moment: every figure shows its cut-off date and its age.

Fuente: https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/ai-classifies-people-decide

## AI classifies and drafts; people decide

Where a language model belongs in a financial product, where it does not, and why the figures should never come from it.

There is a promise repeated in almost every product that adds artificial intelligence: it will do the work for you. It is said of summaries, of recommendations, of answers to business questions. The promise is attractive and, in text tasks, it is often kept. The problem appears when it is extended, without further thought, to money.

The principle we used to design Rovaq AI fits in three clauses, and we consider it a condition of trust and not a limitation: AI helps to organize and to draft; figures come from records that can be verified; and a person decides every action.

### The risk of AI that invents amounts

A language model produces plausible text. That is its strength and also its risk: a sentence can sound exact without being so. If you ask it to summarize a conversation, a minor error hardly matters. If you ask it for an amount, the same kind of error changes a decision.

Besides, the harm is not evenly spread. A tool that is right almost always, but now and then invents an amount, has a worse cost than one that fails often: with the second you know you must verify everything; with the first you stop verifying and the error gets through. Trust is lost at the first report where someone discovers that a figure had nowhere to come from, and earning it back is slow.

### Figures come from the verifiable ledger

The alternative is to separate two jobs that tend to get mixed. One is understanding text: grouping similar conversations, proposing a category, drafting a message. The other is calculating money: adding up refunds, comparing periods, measuring how much revenue is exposed to a problem. The first tolerates some ambiguity and is reviewed by reading. The second does not tolerate it and must be repeatable.

In Rovaq AI, the second job is done by rules and calculations over the organization ledger, which is insert-only and keeps the origin of each record. Every important figure carries its class, its source and its cut-off date, as we explain in [the article on provenance](https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/where-every-number-comes-from). When something is not known, the system says No data; it does not fill the gap with an assumption written with confidence.

The [Ask your data](https://rovaq.ai/en/product/ask-your-data) screen is the clearest example. Today it answers with rules and with read-only tools, without a language model, and it shows the steps it took to calculate each answer. If it does not have the data, it says so. Whoever uses it can follow the calculation and repeat it; they do not have to believe a written answer.

### What AI does today and what it does not

Saying that AI does not create figures does not mean it has no work to do. There are tasks where a model is useful precisely because its output can be read and corrected:

- **Grouping conversations into problems.** Grouping with AI models is enabled per organization, and each group keeps its quotes so that someone can check they really belong there.
- **Classifying.** Proposing a category for a repeated theme, for a person to review.
- **Drafting.** Preparing the draft of a message to a supplier or of an internal note, which a person reviews before sending.

And there are things it does not do. It does not produce amounts. It does not decide what action to take. It does not send anything on its own. It does not write to your CRM, which in the case of HubSpot connects read-only. A draft is a proposal of text, not an action taken. If a draft comes out poorly, it is corrected or thrown away before it reaches anyone.

#### A person decides every action

The last step is always human. In the [To decide](https://rovaq.ai/en/product/to-decide) screen, each proposal arrives with its evidence and its reason, and the person in charge decides what to do with it. The drafts that AI prepares are text that someone reviews and sends; nothing is sent on its own. How a proposal is debated and how its outcome is recorded is another story, which we tell in [the article on decisions](https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/a-recommendation-must-be-debatable).

This split is not a brake. A team reads a draft in seconds, but redoing a wrongly calculated amount can take days. Dividing the work this way puts the speed of the model where a mistake is cheap, in text, and human review where a mistake is expensive, in money and in actions.

### A rule for evaluating any tool

If you are evaluating software with artificial intelligence for your business, three questions help more than any demonstration:

1. Where each amount comes from: a record I can open or a text the model wrote.
2. What happens when information is missing: whether it says so, or fills in the gap with something that sounds reasonable.
3. Who carries out the action: whether a person approves it or it happens on its own.

A tool that answers all three well can still be wrong, like any other, but its errors will be visible and correctable. That is what we aim for by separating clearly what the model does from what stays outside it.

### What we do not claim

- We do not claim that AI makes no mistakes. That is why its proposals are read and a person decides what to do with them.
- We do not claim that Rovaq AI is an autonomous agent: it prepares packages and drafts, and a person decides and files every action.
- We do not claim that grouping with models is on for every organization: it is enabled per organization.
- We do not claim that data is anonymized. Redacting or masking a text is not anonymizing it.
- We do not promise any amount or any financial result as a consequence of a recommendation.

---

Fuente: https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/one-role-one-view

## One role, one view: why each role sees only what belongs to it

A tool with everything for everyone looks generous and delivers little. Showing less protects information and helps people work.

When a team adopts a new tool, the first question is usually what it can do. The second, which is almost never asked in time, is who should be able to do what. When that second question is put off, the result is an application where everyone sees everything: the person carrying out a task stumbles over screens that do not concern them, and whoever reviews the money lives alongside controls they do not need.

The thesis is the opposite one. Showing each person less is not an uncomfortable restriction but a design decision with two benefits: information is better protected and the work is clearer.

### Fewer screens, more clarity

A surplus screen has a cost that does not show in demonstrations. Every additional option is something to understand, ignore or avoid touching by mistake. An operator who has to resolve assigned actions gains nothing from seeing the company financial reports; instead, they lose time searching among items that are not theirs. Fewer options also mean less to learn: a new person starts with what they will actually use.

That is why it helps to design views from the work and not from the menu. The question is not which screens exist, but what the person in each role needs to see to do their own job well. Everything else does not appear.

### Four roles with minimal permissions

Rovaq AI works with four roles. Each one receives what its function requires, and nothing more. A well-designed view is one that removes from each person everything they do not need for their work.

- **[Owner](https://rovaq.ai/en/use-cases/owner).** Configures, decides and approves. Sees all screens and manages the team, the notices and data retention. It is the one who gives the go-ahead to the actions that are proposed.
- **[Analyst](https://rovaq.ai/en/use-cases/analyst).** Investigates, prepares and proposes. Sees the money, the problems, the pain points and the imports, and imports files. Proposes, but does not approve.
- **[Operator](https://rovaq.ai/en/use-cases/operator).** Carries out the actions assigned to them. Sees the problems, the assigned actions and their evidence, without money figures.
- **[Viewer](https://rovaq.ai/en/use-cases/viewer).** Reads with read-only access. Sees the screens that apply to them, unable to modify data, connections or decisions.

The separation between whoever proposes and whoever approves deserves its own mention. That the analyst prepares a finding and the owner approves it is not bureaucracy: it is the way to make sure a different person looks at the evidence before anything is set in motion. And that the operator carries out work without seeing money figures means that whoever does the daily work does not need access to what they do not use.

This split follows a principle known as least privilege: each person receives only the access their function requires. An account with less reach exposes less if something goes wrong, whether a mistake, an oversight or a credential that falls into the wrong hands.

#### A walk-through example

Imagine a shipping problem: several orders on the same route arrive late. The analyst investigates it, gathers the evidence and proposes talking to the carrier. The owner sees the proposal with its evidence and decides whether to accept it, change it or turn it down. If it is accepted, the operator receives the assigned action and carries it out, with the problem and the evidence in view but without the money figures they do not need. And the viewer, if the team has one, can follow the progress with no risk of changing anything.

Each person sees a different part of the same fact and yet nobody needs a complete view to fulfill their role. That is the simplest proof that the split is well made: nobody misses what they do not see, because they did not need it to work.

### Server-side authorization

There is an important difference between hiding and protecting. Many applications hide from the interface the options a user should not use, and consider the matter settled. But an element that does not appear in the menu still exists if someone knows the address of the screen or the way to ask for the data.

In Rovaq AI authorization is decided on the server. Hiding a menu item is a reading convenience; it is not what protects a screen. What we claim and what we do not about security is in [the article on security](https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/what-we-claim-about-security). The decision of whether a person can see a piece of data or carry out an action is taken on the side the user does not control: always on the server.

#### What to ask when evaluating a tool

If you are comparing software for your team, three questions reveal a lot about how it handles permissions:

1. **What each role sees, in writing.** A clear table of capabilities is worth more than a general sentence about security.
2. **Who approves.** If whoever proposes can also approve, review depends on goodwill and not on design.
3. **Where access is decided.** If it is only hidden in the interface, protection is weak; if it is decided on the server, it holds up better.

One question remains that splitting views does not settle on its own: how far to trust what each role reads. That is what our explanation of [the provenance of every number](https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/where-every-number-comes-from) is for: seeing less should not mean knowing less about the origin of what you do see.

### What we do not claim

- We do not claim that minimal permissions eliminate all risk. They reduce what each account can expose, but they do not replace other security practices.
- We do not claim that a role guarantees correct use: a person with access can still make a mistake within what their role allows.
- We hold no security or compliance certifications, and two-step verification for owners is planned; today it is not required.

Fuente: https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/marketplace-exports-are-data

## Your marketplace exports are already data: how to load them with provenance

The files you download from your sales channels are not a pending chore. They are the history you already have, and it can be loaded with its origin in plain view.

Among teams that sell through marketplaces, a common belief spreads: once a direct connection to my channel exists, I will start putting my numbers in order. Meanwhile, sales are downloaded into one sheet, refunds into another, orders into a third, and every month someone pastes them into a workbook that nobody else fully understands.

The wait has a cost that goes unnoticed: those files already hold the history. They are not a step before the data; they are the data. What is almost always missing is not the source, but a place to load them without losing where each line came from.

### What can be loaded today

Today Rovaq AI receives Excel and CSV files. That is the way the data from your sales channels comes in: the exports you already download from each platform, in the format each one produces. Marketplace exports are loaded with help from our team, who go over with you how each column corresponds.

Having support during the load has a practical advantage. Each channel exports its columns in its own way, and the same idea can show up as order, purchase or transaction depending on where it comes from. Settling that correspondence once, with someone who already knows it, keeps a reading error from contaminating months of history.

There is also a reading of conversations from HubSpot, and it is read-only: Rovaq AI does not write to your CRM. The connection is set up with our team and syncing is scheduled, not immediate. In addition, coverage is limited to what the HubSpot API exposes and may be incomplete, so it is wise to read those figures with their cut-off date and that limit in mind.

### Preview and per-row provenance

Loading a file is easy; loading it well is another matter. For an export to be reliable, the load must meet two conditions.

#### First you look, then you load

The load includes a preview and a validation before anything is ingested. Before a single line enters your organization ledger, you can see how the file was read and what would end up loaded, to check that what was read matches what you downloaded. It is the cheap moment to catch that a date came in another format or that a column changed place. Finding out later, with three months of data on top, is expensive.

#### Each row remembers where it comes from

The second condition is keeping the origin. Each loaded row stores which file it came from and which load it entered with, so that any figure can be traced back to the line that produced it. It is the same logic we explained in [the article on provenance](https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/where-every-number-comes-from): a figure is worth as much as its origin, and an origin lost in pasting from one sheet to another cannot be rebuilt later.

This changes the conversation when someone questions a number. Instead of reconstructing from memory which sheet was used, you open the row, see the file and settle it.

### Direct connectors: what does not exist yet

It is worth being clear about what does not exist yet. Direct connectors for Amazon, Walmart and Shopify are planned, but today there is no connection that brings that data in automatically; that is why the route is the export, and why we set no dates or commitments for when it will change.

There are good reasons not to wait. A connector, when it arrives, will bring new data; but your history exists now, and it is exactly what lets you look back: seeing by channel, by product and by month where returned money concentrates, as we describe in [the article on refunds](https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/refund-leak-you-can-locate). Loading the history you already have today does not get in the way of a future connector. What does get in the way is continuing to paste sheets by hand in the meantime.

### How to prepare your exports

Before asking for a load, it helps to review your files with these ideas in mind:

1. Download the original export from each channel and keep it unedited. The file as it left the platform is the most direct evidence of its origin.
2. Note the period each file covers and, if you know it, the date you downloaded it. That will be the cut-off date for what you load.
3. Separate what you download by type: orders, refunds, conversations. Mixing them in one sheet complicates reading.
4. Go through the preview calmly and confirm that columns and dates were read as you expected before approving the load.

A good way to start is with a single channel and a single complete period. If the preview shows what you expected, you repeat the process with the next channel. If something does not add up, you already know where to look, because the scope of the test was small. Going from less to more saves corrections and builds, load after load, a history you can rely on.

None of this requires a long project. With a couple of recent exports you can already answer which channel weighs most in your sales and where each figure that says so comes from, and with that your history stops being a chore and becomes the starting point.

### What we do not claim

- We do not claim that direct connectors with Amazon, Walmart or Shopify exist: they are planned and we give no dates.
- We do not claim that loading marketplace exports is self-service: today it is done with help from our team.
- We do not claim that a channel export contains everything needed. If columns are missing, certain figures cannot be calculated, and the screen says so instead of showing a zero.
- We do not claim that the HubSpot reading covers all your conversations: coverage is limited to what its API exposes and may be incomplete.
- We do not claim that HubSpot updates instantly or that Rovaq AI writes to it: the connection is read-only.

Fuente: https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/pain-points-from-text-to-priority

## Pain points: from free text in conversations to a priority backed by evidence

Counting mentions is a start. A priority also needs a size, evidence that can be opened and a list of what is not known.

In almost any customer support operation there comes a moment when someone reads a hundred conversations and concludes that the problem is shipping. They conclude it because the word shows up a lot. It is a reasonable reading and also the most common way to get a priority wrong.

A theme that repeats in the free text of conversations is a clue, not a priority. To turn it into a priority you need a size, a body of evidence and an honest list of what is not yet known.

### Repeated is not important

Counting mentions is the first thing people try, and it has an obvious appeal: it is quick and it produces an order. The problem is that it measures noise as much as importance. A reason may repeat because it is frequent and cheap, like a question about order status that one line resolves. Another may appear rarely and carry considerable refunds.

There are at least three reasons why the count misleads:

- **The customer language is not the language of your catalog.** Two people describe the same defect with different words, and one word can cover matters that are not alike. Without careful grouping, the count splits one problem across several rows or merges several into one.
- **Frequency is not cost.** A heavily mentioned reason with low impact can rank above a rare and expensive one if all you look at is volume.
- **What gets written most is what is easiest to write.** Channels and forms shape what people complain about and how, so part of the pattern comes from the tool and not from the customer.

None of this invalidates free text. On the contrary, it is the richest source most teams have. What changes is the role it is given: it serves to form hypotheses, not to close them.

> A repeated theme says what people talk about. A priority says how much it weighs and with what evidence.

### Bubble map and size

Moving from a theme to a priority requires answering two questions that the text does not answer on its own. The first is about size: how much this reason weighs and in what unit. The second is about evidence: which conversations and which orders support it, so that another person can open them and check.

Size can be measured in two ways, and it is wise not to mix them. One is volume, meaning how many conversations fall under the reason. The other is the money it carries, when there is a reliable way to link the reason to orders and refunds. A good habit is to look at both and notice where they disagree. A reason that is large in volume and small in money calls for a support response; one that is small in volume and large in money calls for a review of the product or the supplier.

#### Reading both at once

On the [pain points](https://rovaq.ai/en/product/pain-points) screen in Rovaq AI, each bubble is a pain point and its size is returned money in gross dollars or volume, as chosen by whoever is looking. The eight largest appear in the chart and in an accessible table, with a topic filter, and each row opens its evidence down to the source row.

That last part is what turns a map into a working tool. A large bubble that cannot be opened invites argument; a bubble that opens down to the originating conversation and order invites review.

#### What is not known is not zero

On this screen the rule has a concrete consequence: what is not known says No data and never zero, and if a source did not respond, those points show as Not available now. A reason with no reliable link to the money is not a cheap reason, it is an unmeasured one. Why the difference matters so much is explained in [the article on provenance](https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/where-every-number-comes-from); here it is enough to check [data trust](https://rovaq.ai/en/product/data-trust) first and read each number with its source and cut-off date.

### Export without personal data

Prioritizing is rarely the decision of one person. Almost always the finding has to be taken to product, to a supplier or to management, and a tension appears: the most convincing evidence is usually the conversation, and the conversation usually contains data about a customer.

The way out is to separate the two. The evidence export in CSV per pain point is generated without personal data, so it can be shared with whoever needs to see the pattern without information about the writer traveling along. Sharing the evidence should not require sharing the people.

### How to try the method with your conversations

You do not need a new tool to try the method. Take the conversations from a complete period and follow these steps:

1. Group by reason using a written criterion, so another person would group the same way.
2. Measure each group in volume and, where you can link it to orders, in returned money, without mixing the two units.
3. Compare the two rankings and note where they differ; that is usually where the surprise is.
4. For each candidate, gather two or three source conversations that anyone can open and check.
5. Mark what is missing as missing, with the reason, and do not turn it into zero.
6. Take the result to [the decision](https://rovaq.ai/en/product/to-decide): a person chooses what to address and the outcome gets recorded.

### What we do not claim

- We do not claim that a repeated theme is a theme that costs: the screen puts the money it carries beside it only when that money exists.
- We do not promise that every pain point has a money figure: without confirmed links between reasons and orders, the figure is not available and the screen says so.
- We do not determine the cause of a problem: the map orders and shows evidence, and the cause is established by whoever reviews it.
- We do not claim that the map shows every pain point: the chart shows the eight largest.

Fuente: https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/what-we-claim-about-security

## What we claim and what we do not claim about security

A short list of practices, another of gaps and the reasons for publishing both.

A security page is usually the first thing a finance or technology person reviews before accepting a new tool. It is also where statements nobody can verify are most abundant, written with adjectives instead of facts.

Rovaq AI works with support conversations and revenue data from a business, and that obliges us to a specific stance: say what exists, say what does not exist and not fill the space between them with adjectives. Here is that stance and why we believe it serves a buyer better than a promise of total security.

### Practices we describe

We only describe practices that we can point to in the product. Today they are these:

- Each organization is kept apart from the others by rules in the database, not only by the application.
- There are four roles with least-privilege permissions. The platform administration permission is separate and does not grant read access to the business data of other organizations.
- Sign-in is by a link sent to your email, with email confirmation, and sessions use protected cookies.
- Pain-point and claim exports are generated without personal data.
- Administration operations, team changes and retention deletions are recorded.
- Each organization can define retention policies. Before deleting, the screen shows the exact scope and deletes nothing yet.

Each point is written so that it can be checked. Saying that authorization is decided on the server means, for example, that hiding a menu item does not protect a screen: what protects it is the rule applied before the data is handed over.

Describing a practice means that someone can go to the product and check it, and that the sentence was written with that check in mind and not for a sales presentation. A practice that exists only in a sales presentation does not make it onto this list, however attractive it sounds. No external audit has reviewed it: read it as our own description, not as an endorsement.

There is also a rule about artificial intelligence: its outputs are proposals that a person reviews, and nothing is sent or carried out without that person. Where the line falls between what the model does and what it does not is explained in [the article on artificial intelligence](https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/ai-classifies-people-decide).

### Declared gaps

The second list weighs as much as the first. What does not exist yet is this:

- We do not hold SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certification, and we do not claim GDPR compliance.
- No external penetration test has been performed.
- Two-step verification for owners is planned. It is not required today.
- We do not offer single sign-on or a customer-facing audit view.
- There are daily provider backups, without point-in-time recovery, and we make no availability commitments.

Other improvements are planned, such as a strict content security policy that we are still hardening and an audit view. We do not publish dates until we can meet them.

Reading a list of gaps requires telling three things apart: what does not exist, what is planned and what we do not know. What is planned carries no published date. What we do not know is said as such and is not counted in our favor.

An example of the last kind: we have not finished checking in production each of the security headers on the responses, and so we do not claim that the real configuration matches the intended one in every respect. While that check stays open, it is an unknown and we say so.

Deletion also has a limit worth stating: it does not remove the source data in your tool or copies you keep outside Rovaq.

### Why we publish the gaps

There are four reasons, and none is about image.

- A buyer needs to size the risk before signing. Hiding a gap only moves the discovery to a worse moment.
- A claim without limits cannot be checked. A limit can: anyone can verify whether it exists or not.
- It disciplines us. Every sentence in the first list has to survive reading the second, and that discourages the easy adjective.
- It allows an adult conversation. If a buyer requirement depends on something we do not have today, the right answer is to say so, not to argue.

Nor do we claim that what exists is enough for every business. A gap that a team does not care about can be decisive for another, for example when an internal policy requires something we do not have today. In that case the decision belongs to the buyer, and our job is to give the exact information needed to make it.

There is a useful side effect. When a gap is closed, the change can be read against a clear baseline: the list used to say this and now says that. A page that only adds positive sentences does not let you see what changed or when.

> A promise of total security cannot be verified. A list of practices and gaps can.

### How to read a security page

Beyond Rovaq AI, these questions work with any vendor:

- **Facts or adjectives:** every claim should be something you can point to in the product or in a document, not just describe with a qualifier.
- **What is missing:** a page that declares no gap rarely means there is none.
- **Scope and date:** a practice without a review date may describe a state that has already changed.
- **What it does not cover:** copies you keep outside the tool are outside the scope of any deletion by the vendor.

What is described here reflects the state at the time of its publication, the date shown above, and it does not update itself: if something changes later, this text may fall behind.

### What we do not claim

- We do not claim total security or the absence of risk: no vendor can guarantee them.
- We do not claim certifications, regulatory compliance or external audits, because we do not have them.
- We do not claim that data is anonymized.
- We do not claim that the production security configuration has been checked end to end: that check is still open.
- We do not claim that each read of the data is logged: administration operations, team changes and retention deletions are recorded.
- We do not promise availability or product dates.
- We do not present the practices as sufficient for every business: that assessment belongs to the buyer.

Fuente: https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/a-recommendation-must-be-debatable

## A recommendation must be debatable: evidence, approval and outcome

When a proposal brings its evidence, a person who decides and a record of what happened, it stops being an opinion and becomes a habit.

In many teams recommendations die the same way: someone writes them in a document or says them in a meeting, nobody debates them with data and a few weeks later nobody remembers who was going to do what. The suggestion was not bad; it simply had no way of being debated.

A recommendation becomes useful only when it can be questioned: when it brings its evidence into view, has a person who decides and leaves a record of what happened afterward. With that, a suggestion stops being an opinion and becomes a team habit.

### Without evidence it is ignored

A recommendation without support forces the reader to choose between trusting whoever wrote it or distrusting it. Neither stance is a discussion. Trusting without seeing is delegating blindly, and distrusting without seeing is dismissing without criteria. In both cases the business pays the cost.

With evidence the conversation changes. If the proposal states what it observed, where each figure comes from, why that action is suggested and what is expected, the decision maker can disagree with something specific: the source, the period, the assumption or the expectation. That disagreement is exactly what a recommendation should provoke.

Imagine an analyst proposes adding a size guide to a category because the conversations in that category repeat the same reason for exchanges. If the proposal brings the period, the source and the originating conversations, whoever runs the catalog can object that the period is short or that the reason is the material and not the size. The objection improves the decision. Without that data, all that remains is one opinion against another.

A debatable proposal answers four questions:

- What was observed, with the source and the cut-off date of each figure.
- Why this action is suggested and not another.
- What is expected to be achieved, stated so that it can be measured afterward.
- Who will be responsible if the decision is to go ahead.

> A recommendation that cannot be debated can only be obeyed or ignored.

### Proceed, Adjust or Dismiss

The decision needs a small, clear vocabulary. On the [To decide](https://rovaq.ai/en/product/to-decide) screen in Rovaq AI, a person chooses among three answers, and each has defined consequences.

- **Proceed** creates the intervention and the drafts that a person reviews and sends. Nothing is sent automatically.
- **Adjust** asks for a reason, which is recorded.
- **Dismiss** asks for a reason, which is recorded. Reopening a dismissed proposal creates a new event and deletes nothing.

Asking for the reason is not red tape. A dismissed proposal with a stated reason teaches the team which criteria carry weight, and keeps the same idea from starting from zero each time someone proposes it.

Who can do what also matters. The owner, the analyst and the operator can propose; only the owner can approve; the owner and the operator can carry out. Separating proposing from approving lets anyone with a good observation put it on the table without that turning it into an order.

### Record the outcome

Deciding does not end the cycle. Without a record of what happened, the team does not learn and the next recommendation starts again from opinion. That is why the product shows, while a proposal is in progress, who is responsible, what the commitment was, what stage it is in and which drafts exist.

When there is an outcome, it is measured before and after, and only with observed data. That measurement never presents an assumed benefit: if there is no data, the outcome says there is none instead of filling the gap with an optimistic estimate. That discipline is uncomfortable, but it is what makes the record worth keeping.

A useful record also protects whoever made the proposal. If the outcome was not the one expected, the question stops being who got it wrong and becomes which assumption did not hold, which is a question the team can answer and learn from.

It is worth being clear about what is told here. We describe what the product allows you to do, not results obtained with it.

### How to bring it to your team

The method does not depend on a tool. You can start with a shared sheet and these steps:

1. Write each recommendation with the four answers: what was observed, why, what is expected and who answers for it.
2. Decide in a short meeting with one of three outcomes, proceed, adjust or dismiss, and write down the reason.
3. Set from the start how the outcome will be measured, with what data and over what period.
4. Measure before and after with what was observed, and write what could not be measured as not measured.
5. Review dismissed proposals from time to time: some deserve to be reopened, and reopening does not erase what came before.

A good first proposal usually comes from a concrete finding, the kind described in [the article on refunds](https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/refund-leak-you-can-locate) and in [the one on pain points](https://rovaq.ai/en/blog/pain-points-from-text-to-priority), and not from a hunch.

### What we do not claim

- We do not claim that following a recommendation improves results: the product records what happened, it does not guarantee it.
- We show no cases or customer results; this article describes what the product allows.
- We do not promise any financial benefit: the outcome is measured with observed data and, without data, the screen says there is none.
- We do not say that a dismissed proposal is a mistake: it may be the right decision and it should be recorded.
- We do not claim that the product decides for the team: the choice between Proceed, Adjust and Dismiss is made by a person, and nothing is sent or carried out without one.
